name: Marco Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the CNC router and the edge-banding line at Ferreira Furniture, which makes kitchen cabinets. The sheets of board come in, I load the cutting program, check the first panel with a square and tape, and keep the line moving through the day. I start at six. I've been here thirty years, and I'm the one who knows which board warps and which doesn't.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you feel about the newer tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: If it's proven, I'll use it. Last year the office put in a program that turns the customer's drawing into cutting files. I waited until two other shifts had used it for a month. Now I'd not go back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people are getting carried away. At work I'd say it's another tool, like the router was in its day. At church I'd say what I always say, that work is more than a wage, it's how a man looks after his family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not worried. I use a chatbot now and then to convert measurements or translate a supplier's German manual. It's good for that. Real woodwork isn't something it can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as before. I'd go on training the young fellow, Rui, on the router. I'd keep paying into the pension and the savings account. And Ana and I would still plan to stop around 62 and spend more time in the village where I grew up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. There's nothing in it for me to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for small things. A chatbot translated a German manual for the edge-bander in one go, and it saved me a phone call to the supplier. It doesn't know what a board feels like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family make of your plans for retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana, my wife, would like me to stop sooner. My son lives abroad and my daughter is nearby. They both say, Dad, enjoy it, you've earned it.

say: It's **another tool**, like the router was in its day; people are getting carried away.
Work is more than a wage; it's how a man looks after his family.
think: I'm not worried: I use a chatbot to **convert measurements** and translate manuals, nothing more.
Real woodwork isn't something it can do.
do: Carry on as before and keep training **Rui** on the router.
Keep paying into the pension and the savings account.
Plan to stop around 62 and spend time in my **home village**.
feel: **Calm**; there's nothing in it for me to lose.
S0.quote: A chatbot translated a German manual for the edge-bander in one go, and it saved me a phone call to the supplier.
fieldNote: Uses AI only for **small** jobs and keeps a craftsman's pride.
Money and retirement plan give genuine calm.
Values work as duty to family, a traditional frame.

steps.text: Keep running the router and teaching Rui the cutting programs
Add to the pension and savings account every month
Use the chatbot to translate supplier manuals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office goes first. The people who draw up the orders, the buyers who chase board and hardware, and the ones who answer customers. I'd tell the lads on the floor not to laugh, because the floor is next in line, just slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record I think the firm would keep a core of us who know the machines, and get leaner everywhere else. I'm safe for now. But if the owner, Senhor Ferreira, sells to a bigger group, the rules change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get ahead on the new programs, as long as they're proved. I'd ask to be sent on a course for the software that makes the cutting files. I'd keep a few more months of pay in the bank in case. And I'd tell Rui to learn the software side as well as the router, because that's the future of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It isn't me yet, but it changes the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether to trust a new program?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wait until two shifts have used it a month. If it makes a mess of a sheet of oak, I'll hear about it. The proof is on the floor, not in the brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two ladies in the order office, Paula and Inês, are the ones I'd worry about. They've been here fifteen and twenty years.

say: The **office** goes first: the order drawers, the board buyers and customer answerers.
The floor is next in line, just slower.
think: The firm keeps a **core** of us who know the machines and gets leaner everywhere else.
If the owner sells to a bigger group, the rules change.
do: Ask to go on a course for the **cutting file** software.
Keep a few more months of pay in the bank.
Tell Rui to learn the **software** side as well as the router.
feel: **Uneasy**; it isn't me yet, but it changes the place.
S1.quote: If it makes a mess of a sheet of oak, I'll hear about it. The proof is on the floor, not in the brochure.
fieldNote: His **steady** approach: let others prove it, then adopt.
Concern for Paula and Inês, who have long service.
Money is a buffer, so unease is mild.

steps.text: Ask to go on a course for the cutting-file software
Learn the new drawing-to-cutting program once two shifts prove it
Keep three more months of pay in the bank

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for a small firm like ours. At work I'd say, learn the new tools now, because they won't wait. I'd also say that the government has to help companies like Ferreira, or the town loses the factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be worried. In 2028 the office goes. In 2031 a robot that can load the sheets, run the router and stack the panels is a worry, and I'd be 63. I'd say the firm has to buy those robots to survive, but then there's no job for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the software and robot basics, offer to be the person who looks after them. I'd tell Ferreira I'd stay as long as there's a place. I'd save more and cut out the holidays for a couple of years. And I'd talk to Ana about whether we can manage if I stop at 61.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. We'd be okay, but it would feel like the end of something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first in the next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owner for a plan in writing, and I'd go to the parish group and see if any of the other firms are hiring and keeping their people. A town needs its factories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep your place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to stay useful. A man who learns what he needs to and keeps his word will find a place.

say: It's **too fast** for a small firm like Ferreira; learn the tools now because they won't wait.
The government has to help firms like ours, or the town loses the factory.
think: By 2031 a **robot** that loads sheets and runs the router worries me; I'd be 63.
The firm has to buy those robots to survive, but then there's no job for people like me.
do: Learn the software and **robot basics** and offer to look after the machines.
Cut the holidays for a couple of years and save more.
Ask the owner for a **plan** in writing.
feel: **Anxious**; we'd be okay, but it would feel like the end of something.
S2.quote: The firm has to buy those robots to survive, but then there's no job for people like me.
fieldNote: He sees the **bind** facing the owner too: survive by automating.
Responds by offering to maintain robots, a steady-adaptive move.
Asks for a written plan: trust but verify.

steps.text: Take the robot maintenance course and offer to look after the machines
Move extra wages into the savings account each month
Work out with Ana whether we can manage if I stop at 61

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years helps a lot. At work I'd say let's use it wisely, learn what the tools can do, and not wait for a crisis. I'd tell Ferreira to plan the machine upgrades slowly and keep his people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I'd be 63 when the thinking AI arrives, and nearly 66 when the robots do. By then I'd be long retired. It's Rui, who's 27 with a baby on the way, I worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new software, and teach it to Rui and the others, because it's a way to hand on what I know. I'd keep working to 62. I'd put some money into Rui's training if the firm doesn't. And I'd help Ana with her plans to look after her mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. I could see it coming and plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the young fellow, Rui?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to keep learning, and to get his hands on the machine and the screen both. Whoever can do both will keep a place. And I'd tell him to save, even a little, from the first wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything else you'd tell him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also say, don't believe anyone who says it won't affect you. Be ready, but don't be afraid.

say: Five years **helps a lot**; use it wisely and don't wait for a crisis.
I'd tell Ferreira to upgrade slowly and keep his people.
think: I'd be nearly 66 when robots arrive, so I'd be long **retired**.
Rui, who's 27 with a baby on the way, is who I worry about.
do: Learn the new software and **teach it** to Rui and the others.
feel: **Uneasy**, but steady; I could see it coming and plan.
S3.quote: Don't believe anyone who says it won't affect you. Be ready, but don't be afraid.
fieldNote: Time turns his worry into **teaching** Rui what he knows.
Money advice to the young: save from the first wage.
Family duty to Ana's mother is a second claim on his time.

steps.text: Learn the new cutting software and teach it to Rui
Keep running the router line until 62
Help Ana care for her mother after I stop
Pay part of Rui's training course if the firm does not

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a real gift. I'd say it's time for the firm, the town and the school to do it properly. I'd say to the young, learn a skill, learn the new tools, and stay in your community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I'd have been retired eight years, in the village. I won't be on the floor, so it's not my job on the line. It's my grandchildren and Rui's baby I think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 62 or so, then go to the village and help my brother with his olive grove. I'd keep a little aside for the grandchildren. And I'd go to church and the village council, where somebody has to speak about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It lets me finish my working life in peace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you think about most in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandchildren, and Rui's baby. If those two have steady work and a decent town, I'll be content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope for the town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the factory is still there and the town still has work. A town without a factory is a place people leave.

say: Ten years is a **real gift**; the firm, the town and the school can do it properly.
Learn a skill, learn the new tools, and stay in your community.
think: I'd have been **retired** eight years by 2036, so it isn't my job on the line.
It's my grandchildren and Rui's baby I think about.
do: Work until **62**, then help my brother with his olive grove.
Put a little aside for the grandchildren.
Speak up about work at the village **council**.
feel: **Calm**; it lets me finish my working life in peace.
S4.quote: A town without a factory is a place people leave.
fieldNote: The long view lets him settle on **community**: factory, church, village.
Calm because retirement happens before robots arrive.
He wants somebody to speak up about work locally.

steps.text: Work until 62, then retire to the village
Help my brother with his olive grove after I stop
Put aside money for the grandchildren

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's too fast for a small firm and for the people in it. What would help is a government that backs firms that keep their workers, and a plan from the owner that we can read.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I've always trusted proof. Tell me it works, then show me, and I'll use it. I only ask that nobody is pushed out while we find out.

headlineQuote: I've always trusted proof. Tell me it works, then show me, and I'll use it.
portrait: Marco (**58**, CNC router operator at a family cabinet factory) is traditional, church-going and a steady, proof-first adopter.
He uses a chatbot **now and then** for conversions and manuals, and has money and a stop date near 62.
He worries for the office staff, for Rui and for the **town** if the factory fails.
His mood climbs to anxious only when robots reach the router in 2031, and falls back with more time.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries him most because it is too fast for a small firm and its people.
whatWouldHelp: A government that **backs** firms keeping their workers, and a written plan from the owner.
